abstract: Background and Objective Patients with schizophrenia exhibit significant interindividual variations in their response to pharmacotherapy, adverse effects, and clinical outcomes. While once-monthly paliperidone palmitate (PP1M) injections can improve treatment adherence and continuity compared with oral formulations, suboptimal therapeutic outcomes are still observed in some patients. Although the mechanisms underlying the variability in efficacy of long-acting injectables (LAIs) remain unclear, studies suggest an association with alterations in plasma protein expression. This study aims to investigate the correlation between interindividual differences in the response to PP1M treatment and changes in plasma protein abundance using proteomic analysis. Methods This prospective cohort study was conducted in Longgang District, Shenzhen, China. Utilizing Olink Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) proteomics technology, we analyzed plasma samples from 27 healthy controls and 28 patients with schizophrenia who were clinically indicated for and initiated on maintenance therapy with once-monthly paliperidone palmitate long-acting injection (PP1M), as assessed by their treating physicians. Plasma abundance levels of 92 proteins were measured in all patients with schizophrenia, both prior to their first PP1M administration and following at least 3 months of PP1M treatment. Results Our findings demonstrated that maintenance therapy with PP1M for at least 3 months effectively sustained and improved clinical symptoms in clinically stable patients with schizophrenia. However, it was associated with prolactin elevation, a known effect related to paliperidone. Utilizing Olink PEA analysis, we identified 25 plasma proteins, including SNAP23, ENO2, QDPR, ANXA11, and KYAT1, that distinguished patients with schizophrenia from healthy controls. Intriguingly, K -means clustering analysis of the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) across the three groups (healthy controls, pretreatment, and posttreatment) revealed four distinct clusters characterized by specific expression patterns: class 1 (restoration to healthy control levels), class 2 (persistent elevation), class 3 (moderate recovery), and class 4 (further reduction). Analysis of plasma DEPs before and after at least 3 months of PP1M treatment identified significantly altered proteins (ENO2, QDPR, CRKL, ANXA11, KYAT1) exhibiting the class 1 expression pattern, characterized by a progressive restoration of plasma protein abundance to levels observed in healthy controls. Furthermore, analysis of DEPs associated with PP1M-induced hyperprolactinemia (a safety outcome) revealed that patients with schizophrenia demonstrated a higher probability of developing abnormally elevated prolactin levels after at least 3 months of PP1M treatment if they exhibited baseline elevations in ANXA11 and DIABLO, coupled with reduced CLEC5A expression. Conclusions This study reveals transition-associated proteomic signatures in schizophrenia, identifying protein markers that facilitate subgroup stratification and serve as treatment-emergent companion biomarkers to monitor pharmacodynamic shifts during therapeutic transition to PP1M injection therapy. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40263-025-01220-5.
body:
Key Points
Once-monthly paliperidone palmitate long-acting injection (PP1M) maintenance therapy can effectively maintain and improve clinical symptoms in stable patients with schizophrenia, but it may lead to an increase in prolactin levels related to paliperidone.
Following the administration of PP1M, the levels of proteins such as ENO2, QDPR, CRKL, ANXA11, and KYAT1 in plasma were found to return to normal levels observed in healthy individuals, as indicated by protein composition analysis.
The observed plasma protein profile characterized by elevated baseline levels of ANXA11 and DIABLO concomitant with reduced CLEC5A expression in patients undergoing paliperidone treatment may serve as potential predictive biomarkers for subsequent development of hyperprolactinemia.
Introduction
Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder characterized by disturbances in thought, perception, and behavior [
1
]. As reported by the World Health Organization, there are approximately 24 million people globally affected by schizophrenia, with a lifetime prevalence of 0.45% [
2
]. In China, its prevalence is estimated to be 0.6% and 1.1% in rural areas [
3
]. Despite its relatively low prevalence, schizophrenia imposes a significant burden on individuals, families, and society owing to its chronic nature, recurrent episodes, and associated disabilities. Moreover, individuals with schizophrenia have a significantly reduced life expectancy compared with the general population, with males and females experiencing a reduction of 19 and 16 years, respectively [
4
–
7
]. Given the complex nature of schizophrenia, with its unknown etiology and progression, understanding its underlying mechanisms is crucial for developing effective interventions and improving outcomes for affected individuals.
Antipsychotic agents constitute the foundational therapeutic modality for schizophrenia pharmacotherapy, serving critical roles in symptom amelioration and quality-of-life enhancement [
8
,
9
]. Nevertheless, the effectiveness and tolerability of these antipsychotic medications vary significantly among individuals. A substantial proportion of patients experience suboptimal treatment outcomes, including poor adherence, adverse effects, and inadequate symptom control [
9
,
10
]. It highlights the critical role of adherence in optimizing schizophrenia treatment and preventing relapse. Long-acting injectable antipsychotics, such as paliperidone palmitate (PP), offer notable advantages, primarily by enhancing adherence and reducing relapse rates. It has been shown to have a 30% reduction in mortality risk compared with oral formulations of the same medications [
11
,
12
]. Notably, once-monthly paliperidone palmitate long-acting injections (PP1M) is the most commonly prescribed long-acting antipsychotic [
13
–
15
]. Compared with other atypical antipsychotic drugs, paliperidone formulations are effective in managing psychiatric symptoms, improving patient functioning, and reducing relapse rates [
16
,
17
]. However, many patients fail to achieve optimal therapeutic responses despite these improvements while using long-acting antipsychotics [
16
,
18
]. Therefore, to improve treatment outcomes, it is essential to identify the factors contributing to individual variability in response to antipsychotic medications and to develop personalized treatment strategies that address these differences.
Proteomics, the study of proteins and their interactions, offers a promising approach to bridging the gap between genetic variation and phenotypic outcomes. It can identify molecular markers associated with drug response and resistance by analyzing the complete set of proteins expressed in a biological sample [
19
,
20
]. Thus, applying proteomic techniques to study individual differences in antipsychotic drug response may uncover novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, potentially leading to more personalized and effective treatment strategies for mental health disorders. In addition to its role in identifying drug response biomarkers, proteomic biomarkers are also pivotal in elucidating the pathophysiology and progression of schizophrenia [
21
–
23
], offering insights into the molecular alterations underlying the disorder. Recent advancements in proteomics have facilitated the identification of specific protein dysregulations that correlate with schizophrenia [
24
,
25
], enhancing our understanding of its complex biological mechanisms. Thus, these biomarkers not only contribute to a deeper understanding of schizophrenia's pathophysiology but also play a critical role in the early identification, accurate diagnosis, and monitoring of disease progression [
22
,
25
–
28
]. Ultimately, proteomic research holds the potential to improve treatment strategies and provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms driving schizophrenia [
27
].
Emerging evidence proposes that schizophrenia may not be a purely psychiatric disorder but rather a systemic disease [
29
]. Patients with schizophrenia exhibit a substantially higher risk of metabolic disorders compared with the general population [
30
,
31
]. While mainstream perspectives attribute antipsychotic medications as the primary driver of metabolic dysregulation in schizophrenia, alternative viewpoints argue that pharmacological factors alone cannot fully explain this comorbidity. Genomic analyses reveal shared polygenic risk architectures between schizophrenia and metabolic syndrome components, suggesting intrinsic disease-related etiological overlaps [
32
]. Notably, as a pivotal region for mental health prevention and control in Shenzhen, Longgang District documented 8300 registered patients with severe mental disorders in 2017 (registration rate: 4.04‰) [
33
]. The district health authority has integrated free long-acting injectable paliperidone palmitate (PP1M) treatment for eligible patients into its public health policy framework, with full government subsidization of treatment costs. This distinctive clinical intervention paradigm provides a critical real-world foundation for investigating PP1M’s therapeutic mechanisms. Consequently, this study aims to elucidate the potential mediating role of aberrations in metabolism-associated proteins in PP1M treatment outcomes through proteomic profiling, thereby providing scientific evidence for precision management strategies utilizing long-acting injectable antipsychotics.
Materials and Methods
Study Cohort
This prospective cohort study was designed to perform longitudinal molecular phenotyping in patients with schizophrenia undergoing therapeutic intervention with paliperidone palmitate long-acting injectablse. Participants enrollment occurred at the Second People’s Hospital of Longgang District, Shenzhen, China, between August 2023 to December 2023. The cohort included both healthy controls (28 individuals; individuals without any psychiatric disorders) and individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia (30 patients) according to ICD-10 criteria. Following systematic application of inclusion/exclusion criteria, the final study population consisted of 27 healthy controls (one exclusion due to hepatic transaminase elevation exceeding threefold the upper limit of normal [ALT ≥ 3 × ULN]) and 28 patients with schizophrenia (two exclusions: one for ALT ≥ 3 × ULN and one for concurrent ovarian carcinoma).
Inclusion criteria for patients with schizophrenia:
Stable condition;
First-time use of paliperidone palmitate injection;
Prior exposure to risperidone or paliperidone extended-release tablets;
Age ≥ 18 years;
Chinese descent;
No contraindications to paliperidone palmitate injection.
Exclusion criteria for patients with schizophrenia:
Patient with recent electroconvulsive therapy (within the past 2 months);
Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m
2
);
Severe hepatic impairment (AST or ALT ≥ 3 ULN), and transplant etc;
Advanced cancer, severe infections, or other terminal illnesses;
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or pregnancy plans;
Inability to participate owing to medical, geographical, or social factors.
Inclusion criteria for healthy controls:
Aged > 18 and < 80 years;
Absence of psychiatric disorders;
Han Chinese ethnicity without genetic relatedness.
Exclusion criteria for healthy controls:
Diagnosis of any psychiatric disorder including but not limited to: depression, schizophrenia, or mania;
Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m
2
);
Severe hepatic impairment (AST or ALT ≥ 3 ULN), and transplant etc;
Advanced cancer, severe infections, or other terminal illnesses;
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or pregnancy plans;
Inability to participate owing to medical, geographical, or social factors.
Furthermore, this observational study focuses on the treatment of schizophrenia with paliperidone palmitate injection. The decision to use this medication was made on the basis of a comprehensive assessment by the attending physician. All patients with schizophrenia who received paliperidone palmitate (Janssen Pharmaceutica N.V., 1.5 mL) injections followed a standardized treatment regimen, including initial doses (150 mg on the first day, and 100 mg 1 week later at the deltoid muscle) and subsequent monthly maintenance doses (25–150 mg, depending on the patient’s tolerance and/or efficacy, at either the deltoid muscle or the gluteal muscle). Blood samples were collected from patients with schizophrenia both before and after at least 3 months of PP1M treatment (Fig.
1
). The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Longgang District, Shenzhen (LGEY-IRB-KY-2024-001), and all participants had provided informed consent.

A schematic diagram overview of the study. PP1M: once-monthly paliperidone palmitate long-acting injections
Serum or Plasma Preparation
Blood samples were collected from all participants after an overnight fast using siliconized ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) anticoagulant tubes. Healthy control participants underwent blood collection during their routine clinical biochemistry health check. For patients with schizophrenia, blood samples were collected before the initial PP1M injection (either on the same day or within the week prior) and again at least 3 months after initiating treatment. Following collection, blood samples were centrifuged at 4 °C within 2 h to separate plasma and blood cells, which were then aliquoted and stored at −80 °C for subsequent analysis.
Study End Points and Visiting Programs
The primary end point of this study is the recurrence of schizophrenia symptoms at least 3 months after the first use of PP1M. It was assessed by monitoring changes in the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores and the need for additional antipsychotic medication. A PANSS total score reduction rate of ≥ 25% was considered a positive treatment response (PANSS reduction rate = (pretreatment PANSS total score − post-treatment PANSS total score)/(pre-treatment PANSS total score − 30) × 100%). However, if additional antipsychotic medications are required during the follow-up period, regardless of the PANSS score reduction (≥ 25%), the treatment can be deemed ineffective [
34
]. Safety was closely monitored throughout the study. All adverse events and serious adverse events were meticulously recorded. The safety end points focused on metabolic abnormalities, including weight gain, elevated prolactin levels, and dyslipidemia. All efficacy and safety end points were evaluated after at least 3 months of PP1M treatment.
Protein Abundance Measurement
Plasma protein abundance was assessed through Multiplex Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) technology (Olink ProteomicsTM, Sweden). The analysis was performed with Olink Multiplex assays Target 96 Metabolism (V.3045) (
http://www.olink.com
), and real-time PCR quantification was conducted using Fluidigm BioMarkTM HD. PEA technology utilizes a set of antibodies, each attached to a unique DNA oligonucleotide chain, to create highly specific probes. Upon binding to the target substance, these probes trigger the complementary extension of adjacent DNA chains, generating a new DNA template. This template is subsequently amplified via qPCR to enhance the signal for quantitative analysis. Blood plasma samples were mixed and randomly distributed across a 96-well plate to ensure uniform sampling. Each testing plate simultaneously analyzed 88 experimental and 8 control samples for 96 proteins (92 target and 4 internal controls), requiring only 1 μL per panel. The PEA detection technology incorporated a rigorous internal quality control system, including four internal controls per sample to monitor the entire process. The testing panel additionally comprised three interplate controls for data normalization, three negative controls to determine the detection limit, and two sample controls (mixed plasma) for calculating the coefficient of variation.
Specifically, 1 μL of plasma and control samples (1 μL of negative control, 1 μL of sample control, and 1 μL of on-board control) were incubated overnight with 3 μL of culture medium containing antibody probes at 4 °C overnight for antigen–antibody interaction. Following incubation, 96 μL of the extension mixture was introduced, and the reaction underwent 17 cycles of PCR extension and preamplification. Samples were diluted 100-fold to mitigate matrix effects and minimize unpaired oligonucleotide extension. Prior to loading, a 96.96 Dynamic Array™ Integrated Fluidic Circuit (IFC) chip (Fluidigm Corporation, USA) was preconditioned according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The amplified PCR product (2.8 μL) was combined with 7.2 μL of detection reagent, centrifuged at 400×
g
for phase separation, and 5 μL of the supernatant was transferred to sample detection wells. Paired sequence-specific PCR primers were loaded into designated primer wells. The microfluidic process was executed using a Fluidigm IFC controller, followed by quantitative PCR analysis on a BioMark™ HD PCR System. Cycle threshold (Ct) values were normalized against extension controls and negative controls to calculate normalized protein expression (NPX) values through the formula: NPX = log2 (Ct_sample / Ct_control).
The Multiplex PEA quantifies protein abundance in relative terms (NPX) rather than absolute concentrations. NPX represents a log2-transformed arbitrary unit, where a 1-unit increment corresponds to a twofold increase in the target protein concentration (NPX ∝ [Protein]log2). Conversion to absolute pg/mL values requires algorithm-driven normalization as specified in the Olink
®
technical documentation (
www.olink.com/products/complete-biomarker-list
). The limit of detection (LOD) is determined as three times the NPX value exceeding the baseline standard deviation. The specificity of each panel is determined throughout the testing process, where test samples consist of a mixture of full-length recombinant antigens corresponding to 8 out of the 92 proteins in the panel, with only the target proteins yielding signals.
Statistical Analysis
Data analysis and visualization were performed using R software (version 4.4.1) and GraphPad Prism (version 9.0.0). Continuous variables were assessed for normality and presented as mean ± SD for normally distributed data or median and IQR for nonnormally distributed data. Differences between the two groups were analyzed using
t
-tests for normally distributed data or Mann-Whitney
U
/Wilcoxon tests for nonnormally distributed data. Categorical variables were expressed as
N
(%) and compared using chi-square tests or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. For comparisons involving more than two groups, analysis of variance (ANOVA) analysis was employed. Paired Mann-Whitney
U
/Wilcoxon tests were used to assess differences before and after PP1M use. Statistical significance was defined as a
P
-value < 0.05.
Furthermore, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was implemented to evaluate the integrity of plasma protein samples and discriminate intergroup phenotypic variations. Intragroup variability quantification was performed through the computation of the coefficient of variation (CV). Bivariate associations between proteomic signatures and clinical parameters in patients with schizophrenia were examined using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients (
ρ
), where absolute values approaching unity denoted stronger monotonic relationships, with statistical significance determined through null hypothesis testing (
α
= 0.05). Univariate comparative analysis identified differentially expressed proteins across phenotypic strata, employing a significance threshold of
P
<0.05 (two-tailed). Multiple comparison correction was applied via the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to maintain a false discovery rate (FDR) ≤ 0.05. Proteins satisfying both unadjusted
P
< 0.05 and false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted
P
< 0.05 were designated as multivalidated differentially expressed biomarkers.
Results
Metabolic and Clinical Profile of Patients with Schizophrenia Before and after PP1M Treatment
In our study, we included 28 patients with schizophrenia (f/m = 20/8; 71.43%/28.57%, mean age 37 years) and 27 healthy controls (f/m = 18/9; 66.67%/33.33%, mean age 40 years) (Table
1
). Patients with schizophrenia exhibited a significantly higher body mass index (BMI) compared with healthy controls, particularly after 3 months of PP1M treatment, with an average BMI exceeding 28 kg/m
2
. In addition, we observed significantly elevated levels of fasting blood glucose (GLU), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and uric acid (URIC) in the serum of patients with schizophrenia compared with healthy controls (all
P
< 0.05). Interestingly, the prevalence of baseline blood lipid abnormalities was significantly lower in the schizophrenia group (3.57%) compared with the healthy control group (23.08%,
P
= 0.0216). Moreover, throughout the follow-up study, there was a significant decrease in the proportion of participants using risperidone after switching to PP1M (3.57% versus 71.43%,
P
< 0.0001). This reduction may be attributed to the fact that many participants were undergoing risperidone desensitization at baseline.

Changes in PANSS Scores in Patients with Schizophrenia following PP1M Treatment

35
]. In the present study, all patients with schizophrenia underwent PANSS assessments at baseline, before, and after the end point visit. Changes in PANSS total and factor scores from baseline to the end point visit are presented in Table
2
. After at least 3 months of PP1M treatment, significant improvements were observed in PANSS total score, positive, negative, and general psychopathology subscales compared with baseline (all
P
< 0.05).

Safety and Tolerability of PP1M
PP1M was generally well-tolerated, although it was associated with some adverse events. In our study, we did not observe any deaths of the patients. However, 12 patients (42.86%) exhibited elevated prolactin levels at the end point visit, with a higher prevalence in females (10/12). In addition, 12 patients (42.86%) had persistently abnormal prolactin levels throughout the study. Menstrual disturbances were reported in six cases (21.42%). Regarding adverse events, extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) were observed in six patients (21.43%), including tremors, akathisia, muscle rigidity, and dystonia. Persistent injection site pain for at least 3 days was reported in three patients (10.71%). On average, patients experienced a mean (SD) weight gain of 1.63 (4.40) kg, with eight8 patients (28.57%) gaining ≥ 3% of their body weight (Supplementary Table
S1
).

To identify a plasma profile that could both identify individuals at high risk for schizophrenia and stratify high-risk populations, we cross-analyzed baseline differential plasma proteins between the schizophrenia group and healthy controls and among subgroups. We found that THOP1 and TYRO3 were significantly elevated in patients with schizophrenia and exhibited sex-specific differences. Furthermore, TYMP, ENPP7, ALDH1A1, and THOP1 were significantly correlated with BMI, while ENO2, CRKL, CDHR5, and IGFBPL1 were significantly correlated with age (Supplementary Fig. S2B). These proteins represent potential plasma biomarkers that could be used to identify individuals at high risk for schizophrenia in population screening, and to stratify patients during therapeutic transition to PP1M injection therapy for optimized personalized management.

Baseline Plasma Protein Profile is Associated with Abnormally Elevated Prolactin Levels
In the present study, we found elevated prolactin in 24 patients with schizophrenia. Furthermore, to investigate the association between plasma protein profiles and changes in prolactin levels induced by 3 months of PP1M treatment, we identified two distinct subgroups of patients with schizophrenia: the new-onset elevated prolactin group, which include 12 out of 24 patients with schizophrenia with normal baseline prolactin levels and who developed hyperprolactinemia after PP1M treatment, and the prolactin level normalization group, which was comprised of 12 out of 24 patients with schizophrenia with baseline hyperprolactinemia, had experienced a reduction in prolactin levels post-PP1M treatment.
Furthermore, univariate analysis of the new-onset elevated prolactin group revealed significant decreases in eight proteins (SNAP23, GRAP2, SERPINB6, PPP1R2, CRKL, ANXA11, CA13, DIABLO) and a significant increase in CLEC5A after PP1M treatment (Fig.

Discussion
Our study demonstrates that alterations in plasma protein expression in patients with schizophrenia during transition to PP1M injection therapy may reflect transition-associated proteomic signatures. Using Olink PEA proteomics, we identified 25 proteins that were differentially expressed in patients with schizophrenia compared with healthy controls. Moreover, we observed that short-term PP1M treatment elicited significant pharmacodynamic shifts in protein expression levels. Stratified analyses by age and prolactin levels further suggested that these transition-associated proteomic signatures may aid in characterizing patient heterogeneity and the pharmacodynamic response following the transition to PP1M injection therapy, highlighting their potential utility in guiding personalized therapeutic approaches during this specific treatment phase.
Schizophrenia is a chronic, highly recurrent, and severely disabling mental disorder, while antipsychotic medication is the primary treatment for alleviating clinical symptoms and improving patients’ quality of life [
37
–
40
]. Studies have demonstrated that long-acting injectable antipsychotics, compared with oral formulations, can not only prevent relapse and significantly reduce rehospitalization risk but also promote symptom relief, improve social functioning and quality of life, and lower mortality. Furthermore, they can significantly enhance treatment adherence and continuity [
39
,
41
–
43
]. Paliperidone, with its rapid onset of action, relatively few adverse reactions, and significant improvement in both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, as well as its ability to increase treatment adherence, has been used for both the acute and maintenance phases of the disorder [
44
]. However, mental illnesses exhibit high heterogeneity, with significant individual differences in drug efficacy, adverse reactions, and disease prognosis. Studies have shown that some patients still experience poor efficacy after using long-acting paliperidone formulations, yet the reasons for these individual differences in treatment effects remain unclear [
45
,
46
]. As a long-acting benzisoxazole-derived atypical antipsychotic, the therapeutic mechanism of paliperidone palmitate, though not fully elucidated, is predominantly attributed to its polypharmacological profile involving coordinated multi-receptor interactions [
47
]. Current evidence indicates that its principal antipsychotic efficacy arises from differential receptor antagonism—demonstrating higher potency at serotonin 5-HT
2A
versus dopamine D
2
receptors [
48
], with additional activity at adrenergic α
2
and dopamine D
3
receptors [
49
,
50
]. This multitarget engagement underlies its balanced improvement of both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. As mechanistically corroborated, our results demonstrated that monthly injections of paliperidone palmitate (PP1M) significantly improved symptoms in patients with schizophrenia, as evidenced by reductions in PANSS total, positive, negative, and general psychopathology subscale scores. These findings are consistent with previous studies, including a large international multicenter study that reported that 9.2% of patients with first-episode schizophrenia who switched from oral medication to PP1M for over 12 months achieved a ≥ 20% reduction in PANSS total scores, and 47.2% achieved a ≥ 50% reduction from baseline [
51
].
Furthermore, our study supports the efficacy of PP1M in improving specific symptom domains, as measured by the Marder factor scores, because we observed significant improvements in negative symptoms, cognitive deficits, excitement, hostility, and anxiety depression, as reported previously [
52
–
54
]. Disturbances in the fronto-temporal cortical networks have consistently been associated with negative symptoms. Studies demonstrate that second-generation atypical antipsychotics enhance dopamine release specifically in the prefrontal cortex rather than the nucleus accumbens of the limbic system, potentially attributable to their potent 5-HT2A receptor antagonism combined with weaker D2 receptor blockade (a pharmacological profile exemplified by paliperidone’s receptor affinity) [
55
]. Similar to lithium and valproate, paliperidone exerts mood-stabilizing effects by modulating the expression levels and phosphorylation of complex I and V proteins in synaptic neuropreparations from rat prefrontal cortex [
56
]. These mechanistic hypotheses and findings align closely with our research observations of significant improvements in negative symptoms, excitement, hostility, and anxiety-depression comorbidity. Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that beyond conceptual overlap, negative symptoms and cognitive impairment may share underlying mechanisms, including aberrant interhemispheric connectivity (particularly within the globus pallidus), neurotransmitter dysregulation, and impaired neuronal plasticity [
57
,
58
]. This mechanistic convergence might explain the concurrent improvement of cognitive function alongside amelioration of negative symptoms. In contrast, the lack of substantial change in positive symptoms may be attributed to PP1M’s relatively mild sedative effects [
59
–
62
]. However, despite this, the overall reduction in psychiatric symptoms has the potential to lower the reliance on sedative-hypnotic medications [
18
]. Moreover, these findings suggest the clinical efficacy of PP1M and the use of long-acting injectable antipsychotics, such as PP1M, as a valuable treatment option for both the acute and maintenance phases of schizophrenia.
In addition, we observed significant increases in prolactin levels (PRL) and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at the follow-up end point, alongside an average weight gain of 1.63 kg from baseline, which aligns with prior studies examining PP1M’s safety profile [
63
–
65
]. Paliperidone exerts inhibitory effects on receptors such as 5-HT, DA, and H1 in vivo, potentially disrupting neurotransmitter homeostasis. Current evidence suggests that antipsychotic-induced metabolic disturbances are closely linked to such neurotransmitter imbalances [
66
]. Animal studies indicate that activating 5-HT receptors may alleviate olanzapine-induced hyperphagia and improve insulin resistance, whereas antagonizing hypothalamic H1 receptors stimulates appetite, promotes fat accumulation, and reduces energy expenditure, ultimately contributing to weight gain [
67
]. In addition, blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in neural pathways such as the mesolimbic and mesocortical systems (including D2 receptors on anterior pituitary prolactin-secreting lactotroph cells) attenuates dopamine’s inhibitory effect on prolactin secretion, leading to elevated prolactin levels. However, patients transitioning from oral antipsychotics to long-acting injectables (LAIs) experienced a higher incidence of EPS and injection site pain compared with similar regional studies, which may be attributed to differences in sample size and concomitant medication regimens [
68
,
69
]. Notably, PP1M may have a beneficial impact on liver and kidney function, as evidenced by significant decreases in ALT, AST, and uric acid levels after switching from oral antipsychotics, further supporting the safety profile of PP1M, and making it a suitable option for long-term treatment of schizophrenia.
Plasma proteomics offers a promising approach to identifying protein biomarkers that can improve disease diagnosis and treatment. Researchers can identify specific markers that reflect disease states by analyzing the protein profiles in blood plasma, leading to more accurate and timely diagnoses [
20
,
70
]. Current evidence supports the existence of bioenergetic metabolic dysfunction in patients with schizophrenia, and such metabolic abnormalities may further disrupt both structural connectivity and functional network integration patterns within the brain [
71
]. Our proteomic analysis revealed that patients with schizophrenia could be stratified on the basis of their response to PP1M treatment and susceptibility to adverse effects. Moreover, factors such as BMI, age, and gender were found to influence treatment outcomes. It suggests personalized treatment strategies based on proteomic biomarkers may improve patient outcomes and minimize adverse effects. Our results identified 25 plasma proteins that differentiate individuals with schizophrenia from healthy controls, with KYAT1, ENO2, and CRKL showing the most significant differences, which may aid in early detection of the disease on the basis of protein profiles. This notion is aligned with previous findings that suggested KYAT1, CLEC5A, and RTN4R as biomarkers for schizophrenia. For instance, kynurenine aminotransferase 1 (KYAT1), a key enzyme in the kynurenine metabolic pathway, converts kynurenine to kynurenic acid (KYNA) and has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia [
72
]. Similarly, CLEC5A, a C-type lectin receptor, has been implicated in neuroinflammation [
73
], while RTN4R plays a crucial role in axonal growth and synaptic plasticity [
74
]. Both of these factors are essential for normal brain development, and disruptions in these processes may contribute to the neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with schizophrenia [
75
,
76
]. While previous research has primarily focused on genetic variations, our study highlights the importance of protein expression changes in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia. We propose that alterations in proteins such as KYAT1, CLEC5A, and RTN4R may contribute to the development of the disorder. Further research is needed to validate these findings in larger and more diverse populations.
Furthermore, our study demonstrates that PP1M treatment modulates the expression of several proteins, including ENO2, QDPR, CRKL, ANXA11, and KYAT1. The decrease in ENO2, a glycolytic enzyme, following PP1M treatment aligns with previous in vitro findings [
77
]. These studies suggest that increased ENO2 expression may contribute to the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, and our in vivo findings further support this hypothesis. In addition, changes in CRKL, a protein implicated in schizophrenia expression, have been observed in animal models treated with antipsychotic drugs, indicating a potential common mechanism of action. For instance, in mouse models, aripiprazole and risperidone have been shown to regulate the phosphorylation status of CRKL, suggesting that different antipsychotic drugs may share a common molecular mechanism of action [
78
]. However, identifying QDPR, ANXA11, and KYAT1 as key components of the transition-associated proteomic signature reflecting pharmacodynamic shifts during PP1M therapy is a novel finding in our study. Combining these findings with our stratified analysis, we observed that ENO2 and CRKL levels were associated with age, while ANXA11, DIABLO, and CLEC5A levels were linked to prolactin levels. The association between psychiatric disorders and oxidative stress is well-established [
79
], with antipsychotic treatments (including risperidone and paliperidone) potentially triggering endogenous oxidative imbalance [
80
]. Mitochondria, the organelles most vulnerable to oxidative stress, are significantly impacted. SMAC/DIABLO, a mitochondrial proapoptotic protein, exhibits increased expression under oxidative stress, thereby promoting mitochondrial apoptosis [
81
,
82
]. Conversely, mitochondrial dysfunction further exacerbates oxidative stress. Elevated prolactin (PRL) levels may mitigate oxidative damage by reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production through mechanisms such as enhancing cell survival, suppressing apoptosis, and preserving mitochondrial function, while also exerting antiinflammatory effects [
83
–
85
]. Our study identified a positive correlation between PRL and DIABLO levels, suggesting that PRL elevation might represent a compensatory response to counteract DIABLO-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis and aggravated oxidative stress. Intriguingly, reduced baseline CLEC5A expression was associated with decreased ROS and proinflammatory factor levels [
86
], conflicting with the hypothesis that heightened oxidative stress and inflammation trigger protective PRL elevation. This paradox implies that PRL concentrations may exert completely opposing effects depending on the pathophysiological context. These findings suggest personalized treatment strategies based on specific protein biomarkers may improve patient outcomes. For instance, monitoring ENO2 and CRKL levels could guide treatment decisions in different age groups, while monitoring ANXA11, DIABLO and CLEC5A levels could help manage prolactin-related side effects. Further research is needed to validate these findings and develop targeted therapeutic approaches.
Limitations of the Study
Although this study provides valuable insights into plasma proteomic signatures during the therapeutic transition in schizophrenia, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the relatively small sample size limits the generalizability of our findings; future validation through larger-scale, multicenter studies in broader populations is warranted. Second, the exclusive use of the Olink PEA platform for proteomic analysis necessitates cross-validation of candidate biomarkers by integrating multiplatform technologies such as mass spectrometry. Third, the open-label design may introduce assessment bias, potentially influencing subjective evaluations by both patients and physicians—a factor that should be addressed in future research designs. Fourth, although major demographic variables were controlled, we did not comprehensively analyze the impact of potential confounding factors (e.g., metabolic indices such as BMI and blood glucose, or concomitant medications) on protein expression; subsequent studies should establish more robust variable control models. Finally, the causal relationships between these transition-associated protein biomarkers and disease pathogenesis, as well as treatment response to PP1M, require further elucidation through experimental investigations.
Conclusions
This study demonstrates the potential of plasma proteomics to advance the diagnosis and management of schizophrenia through transition-associated proteomic signatures. By identifying 25 proteins that differentiate patients with schizophrenia from healthy controls, we have uncovered novel biomarkers for early disease detection. Furthermore, our analysis of protein expression changes during therapeutic transition to PP1M injection therapy indicates that specific proteins (such as ENO2, QDPR, CRKL, ANXA11, KYAT1) may serve as companion biomarkers reflecting pharmacodynamic shifts. In addition, stratified analysis reveals that protein profiles correlated with age and prolactin levels are associated with differential treatment responses. These findings provide a framework for developing personalized treatment strategies, paving the way for optimized patient-specific care in schizophrenia.
